newsitem.title: USA: Alaska gov proposes dropping jet-fuel tax.
newsitem.headline: Alaska gov proposes dropping jet-fuel tax.

text.p: Alaska Gov. Tony Knowles on Wednesday proposed eliminating the state tax on jet fuel used by international carriers that stop in Alaska on their way to other U.S. destinations.
If passed by the state legislature next year, the governor's proposal would allow international carriers to escape the 3.2 cent-per-gallon state tax imposed on jet fuel.
"What I'm proposing is to drop the state fuel tax that we put on international carriers that stop in Alaska and then go onto other domestic ports," Knowles said during a visit to Fairbanks.
The plan would allow Alaska refineries to better compete with out-of-state refineries, said Knowles, a Democrat.
The federal government currently allows carriers to buy tax-free fuels through free trade zones or transit from refineries in some parts of the lower 48 states, he said.
"If we're going to be competitive, we're going to have to be able to match what they can get produced by refineries elsewhere," Knowles said.
The tax generated about $3.2 million last year for the state, most of it paid by Mapco, Petro Star and other in-state refineries, Knowles said.
The governor's proposal was welcomed by Jeff Cook, Mapco's chief executive.

"There is a lot of growth potential in the jet fuel market. This will encourage Mapco to expand in-state production at the expense of imported fuel," Cook said in a news release issued by the governor's office.
The change could also help draw more international flights to Alaska, Knowles said.

During a trade mission to Asia last week, the governor and other state officials tried to convince Japan's All Nippon Airways and the U.S. carrier Northwest Airlines to resume direct air service between Japan and Alaska.
Until they do so, Japanese tourists wanting to visit Alaska must fly through Seattle or Seoul, instead of taking a six- or seven-hour direct flight.
